screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Operators
screens.subtitle: How C# stores, classifies, and transforms game data

narration.text: In this lesson we will build a practical foundation for working with data in Unity using C#. Variables are the named containers your game uses to remember values like scores, positions, and state flags. You will learn how to declare those containers, choose an appropriate data type, and apply operators to read and change values. We will use concrete game examples such as player score, move speed, and a player position represented as a three-component vector. You will also see Unity-specific types that make spatial and visual data simple to work with. Knowing when to use an int versus a float, or a Vector3 versus separate floats, changes correctness, performance and how you communicate intent to team members. Along the way we'll point out common pitfalls, like integer division and confusing assignment with comparison, and show how scope affects where a variable can be used. By the end of the chapter you will be able to declare variables, inspect public fields in Unity's Inspector, use arithmetic and logical operators, and reason about scope. Think about one value in your current project and how choosing its type would change how you write code and test behavior.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Variables hold values of a specified data type; operators let you compute and change those values; Unity adds types like Vector3 and Color for common game data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you'll develop four concrete abilities. First, you will define and declare variables in C# so they reliably hold and communicate game data. That means writing member fields and local variables and initializing them with sensible defaults. Second, you'll identify primitive C# data types like int, float, bool, and string, and pick the right one for scores, positions, state flags, and UI text. Third, you will understand Unity-specific structures such as Vector3, Quaternion, and Color, and when to use them to represent positions, rotations and colors instead of separate floats. Fourth, you'll apply operators — arithmetic, assignment, comparison and logical — to compute values and to build conditions that drive gameplay. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to help you remember the difference between declaration, type, and scope. We will verify competency by showing how public fields appear in the Inspector and by walking through sample code that changes variables at runtime. Keep an eye out for common mistakes such as integer division and using assignment when you meant comparison. These objectives guide hands-on practice and help you make safe choices in real projects.

screens.title: What is a Variable?
screens.subtitle: A named storage location that holds a value of a defined type

narration.text: A variable is a named storage location in memory that holds a value of a specific type. Think of it as a labeled box: the label is the variable name and the box contents are the value. In Unity C#, variables let scripts remember things like player score, whether a door is open, or the player's name. Declaring a variable ties a name to a data type; that type determines valid operations and how the runtime stores the value. For example, declaring playerScore as an int reserves space for a whole number and signals that arithmetic like addition and subtraction is appropriate. A concrete example from the PlayerManager script is public int playerHealth = 100; which creates a member variable with an initial value. A common misconception is that variable names determine behavior — they only help readability. The actual behavior depends on the data type and how you use operators on the variable. Another confusion is thinking all variables are visible in the Inspector; only public (or serialized) fields are shown. Key takeaway: use clear names and the correct type to encode intent and avoid later casting or conversion errors. Which piece of game data in your project would be best represented as a variable, and what type would you choose?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A variable is a named place in memory with a specific data type that determines what values and operations are allowed.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is a Variable?
What is a Variable?
A named storage location that holds a value of a defined type.
Definition & Analogy
A variable is like a labeled box where you put a value. The label is the name and the type is the label on the box telling you what can go inside. Using clear names and the right type reduces confusion and prevents errors when you manipulate values later.
Example
public int playerHealth = 100; creates a member variable that stores a whole number representing health.
Misconception
Names do not change behavior; the declared data type and used operators determine what a variable can do.
Key Takeaway
Declare variables with clear names and correct types to make code intentional and safe.
Concrete Scenario
Imagine a scoreboard: score, highScore, and playerName. Choosing int for score and string for playerName ensures you can run arithmetic on score and display playerName as text. If you used string for score you would need to convert types before arithmetic, which is error-prone.
Check Your Understanding

screens.title: Declaring and Initializing Variables in C#
screens.subtitle: Member fields, local variables, and default values

narration.text: Declaring a variable ties a name to a data type and, optionally, an initial value. In Unity scripts you usually declare member fields inside the class but outside methods so they persist for the object's lifetime. For example, public int playerScore = 0; exposes the field in the Inspector and initializes it. Inside methods, such as Start(), you use local variables for temporary calculations, like int enemiesDefeated = 0;. Local variables exist only while the method runs. Initialization matters: an uninitialized field gets a default value, but local variables must be initialized before use. A practical example from the PlayerManager activity is setting currentPosition = new Vector3(0, 0, 0); to give a clear starting point for movement calculations. A common mistake is expecting a local variable to retain a value across frames; it will not. Another confusion is assuming public means global — public makes the field visible to other classes and the Inspector, but scope remains tied to the class instance. The best practice is to declare member fields for state you need across methods, initialize them consciously, and use local variables for step-by-step calculations. Which variables in your scripts should be member fields rather than local temporaries?

keyIdea.title: Declaration pattern
keyIdea.text: Declare member fields for persistent state and local variables for temporary calculations. Initialize to avoid undefined behavior.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Declaring and Initializing Variables
Declaring and Initializing Variables
Member fields versus local variables and why initialization matters.
Code Example
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public string playerName = "New Player";
    public int playerHealth = 100;
    public float moveSpeed = 5.0f;
    public bool canMove = true;
    public Vector3 currentPosition;

    void Start()
    {
        currentPosition = new Vector3(0, 0, 0);
        int bonus = 50; // local variable
        playerHealth += bonus;
        Debug.Log("Health: " + playerHealth);
    }
}
Notes & Example
  • Member fields are defined on the class and persist across methods and frames.
  • Local variables live only inside a method and are useful for temporary calculations.
  • Initialize currentPosition to a defined Vector3 so movement code has a known start point.
Common Mistake
Expecting a local variable to persist across frames or methods can cause incorrect state assumptions.
Key Takeaway

Use member fields for persistent state and initialize values to avoid undefined behavior.

screens.title: Primitive Data Types in C#
screens.subtitle: int, float, bool, and string with game examples

narration.text: C# supplies primitive types that are the building blocks of game data. int stores whole numbers and suits values like playerHealth, score, or ammo count. float stores decimal numbers required for physics and positions, such as moveSpeed and distance — remember to use the literal suffix when writing floats in code. bool stores true or false state flags like isAlive or canMove, and string stores text such as playerName or UI messages. Each type determines which operations work directly; you can add two ints or two floats but you cannot perform arithmetic on a string without converting it. A concrete example: if you write int health = 100; and then health = health - 20; the result is another int. A common pitfall is integer division: dividing two ints truncates decimals. For instance, 5 divided by 2 is 2 as an int. If you need fractional results, make one operand a float. Another practical note is memory and intent: choosing float for fractional values signals to teammates that decimals are expected. Practice by assigning sample values in PlayerManager and observe the console output. Which variable in your project most often requires decimals and should therefore be a float?

keyIdea.title: Primitive types
keyIdea.text: int for whole numbers, float for decimals, bool for true/false, string for text — pick based on the value and its operations.

Type Reference

screens.title: Unity-Specific Types: Vector3, Quaternion, Color
screens.subtitle: Structures that model spatial and visual data

narration.text: Unity provides specialized structures to represent common game data: Vector3, Quaternion, and Color. Vector3 groups three floats into a single value and is commonly used for positions, scales, and Euler angles. Using Vector3 for transform. position means you can assign, interpolate, and pass position data as a single coherent object. Quaternion represents rotation in a way that avoids gimbal lock and enables smooth rotation math; many Unity APIs expect Quaternions for setting rotation. Color groups components for red, green, blue and alpha, each as floats from zero to one, making it easy to tint materials or UI elements. A concrete example is public Vector3 playerPosition = new Vector3(0, 1, 0); which sets an initial world position. A common misconception is to treat Vector3 as three independent floats; preferring unified types helps you use Unity methods directly and prevents mismatches. When you store position as three floats you lose the convenience of passing a single Vector3 to APIs like transform. Translate. Key takeaway: use Unity structures when they match the data domain to leverage built-in engine behaviors and APIs. How might representing rotation with Quaternion change how you animate an object compared to Euler angles?

keyIdea.title: Unity structs
keyIdea.text: Vector3, Quaternion, and Color encapsulate multi-component values so Unity APIs can operate on them directly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Unity-Specific Types
Unity-Specific Types
Vector3, Quaternion and Color let Unity APIs handle complex values.
Vector3
Represents x, y, z floats. Use for positions and directions. Example: new Vector3(0,1,0).
Quaternion
Represents rotation without gimbal lock. Prefer for smooth rotation math and many transform APIs.
Color
Stores r, g, b, a floats in range 0 to 1. Example: Color.green or new Color(1f, 0f, 0f, 1f).
Practical Note
Using these structures lets you pass a single value into engine methods. For instance, transform.position accepts a Vector3, so keeping position as a Vector3 avoids conversions and keeps intent clear.

screens.title: Public vs Private and the Inspector
screens.subtitle: How access modifiers affect visibility and workflow

narration.text: Access modifiers control who can see and change a variable. In Unity, declaring a field as public exposes it on the Inspector for a given GameObject, making it easy for designers to tweak values without changing code. Private fields are hidden from other classes and the Inspector unless explicitly serialized. For example, public float moveSpeed = 5.0f; appears on the GameObject so you can tune it in the editor. The process is simple: declare the public field, save the script, attach it to a GameObject, and observe the field in the Inspector. A common misconception is that public means global; in fact it refers to visibility across classes, not lifetime or scope. Another pitfall is relying only on Inspector values for critical initialization; always set sensible defaults in code and use the Inspector for tuning. For collaborative projects, exposing only the fields that designers need keeps interfaces clean. Practice by making playerColor public and changing it in the Inspector to see immediate effects. How will you decide which fields to expose for your team to adjust? Public vs Private and the Inspector means public fields appear in the inspector for editing at design time; private fields do not unless serialized. use public for designer-tweakable parameters.. In practical terms, how access modifiers affect visibility and workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inspector workflow
keyIdea.text: Public fields appear in the Inspector for editing at design time; private fields do not unless serialized. Use public for designer-tweakable parameters.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Public vs Private
Public vs Private and the Inspector
Decide which fields designers should edit and which should remain internal.
Process
  1. Declare public field in the script: public float moveSpeed = 5.0f;
  2. Save and attach the script to a GameObject.
  3. Select the GameObject and edit the field in the Inspector to tune values.
Example
Make playerColor public to allow designers to change color per instance in the Inspector.
Notes & Pitfalls
Public exposes to other classes and the Inspector, but it does not make a value global. Use [SerializeField] for private fields you still want visible in the Inspector.
Key Takeaway

Expose only the fields you want designers to tune and keep implementation details private to prevent misuse.

screens.title: Operators Overview
screens.subtitle: Categories: arithmetic, assignment, comparison, and logical

narration.text: Operators are symbols that perform operations on values or variables. There are four categories you will use frequently in Unity scripts. Arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) compute numerical results and are the basis of health, movement and scoring calculations. Assignment operators (=, +=, -=, *=, /=) place or update values in variables, where shorthand helps keep code concise. Comparison operators (==,!=,, =) compare values and yield booleans for conditional checks. Logical operators (&&, ||,!) combine or invert booleans to form composite conditions. For example, playerScore += 10; increases score by ten. A practical conditional could be if (playerScore >= 100) { Debug. Log("Player reached a high score!"); } which uses comparison to decide when to print a message. A common error is using assignment when comparison was intended, which changes state instead of checking it. Another gotcha is the modulo operator for cycling or tests like even/odd. Operators are the tools that transform and test your data; practice them by updating playerHealth, computing speed from distance and time, and combining flags to decide whether movement is allowed. Which operator category do you find yourself using most in gameplay code?

keyIdea.title: Operator categories
keyIdea.text: Arithmetic to compute, assignment to store, comparison to test, logical to combine truths—together they let your game change and decide.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Operators Overview
Operators Overview
How operators let you compute, store, compare and combine values.
Arithmetic
+, -, *, /, %
Assignment
=, +=, -=, *=
Comparison
==, !=, <, >, <=, >=

Common Mistake
Using = inside a conditional when you meant == changes the variable instead of comparing it.

screens.title: Arithmetic Operators and Modulo
screens.subtitle: Use arithmetic for movement, health and scoring; modulo for cycles

narration.text: Arithmetic operators let you calculate in-game values. Use + and - for adding or subtracting quantities such as score or health. Use * and / for scaling and averaging, as when computing speed from distance and time. The modulo operator returns the remainder of a division and is handy for cyclic logic. For instance, using % to cycle through animation frames or to check for even or odd numbers is common. A concrete example is int health = 100; int attackDamage = 20; health = health - attackDamage; which reduces health by twenty. Another practical example is float calculatedSpeed = distance / time; where at least one operand should be a float to avoid integer truncation. For modulo, int remainder = 5 % 2; yields 1, which can be used to alternate behavior every other frame. A misconception is expecting modulo to produce fractional remainders; modulo works with integers in this context. Practice by applying damage with subtraction, boosting speed with multiplication, and using modulo to make an event happen every three updates. The real insight is choosing the right operator to express intent and avoiding integer division when fractional results are needed.

keyIdea.title: Arithmetic uses
keyIdea.text: Use + - * / for numeric math and % to compute remainders or cycles; use floats when you need fractional results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Arithmetic Operators
Arithmetic Operators and Modulo
Common numeric operations and when to use modulo.
Code Walkthrough
int health = 100;
int attackDamage = 20;
health = health - attackDamage; // health is now 80

float distance = 15.0f;
float time = 3.0f;
float calculatedSpeed = distance / time; // 5.0f

int remainder = 5 % 2; // 1
Guidance
  • Use subtraction to apply damage and addition to give rewards.
  • Use multiplication to scale speed or apply power-ups.
  • Use modulo to trigger periodic events or test parity.
Practice
Make a counter that increments each Update and logs a message every third frame using %.

screens.title: Assignment Operators and Shorthand
screens.subtitle: Keep code concise and expressive with compound assignments

narration.text: Assignment operators place values into variables and compound forms provide shorthand. The basic assignment operator equals stores the right-hand value into the left-hand variable. Compound assignments combine an arithmetic operation and assignment in one step, such as playerScore += 10; which adds ten to playerScore. Other forms include -=, *=, and /=. This pattern keeps code concise and reduces repetition. A concrete example is playerSpeed *= 1.2f; to apply a speed boost multiplicatively. Be careful with the order of operations and types: playerScore += 10; implicitly performs addition compatible with the declared type. A common misconception is that compound operators always create a new type; they operate on the existing variable type and can cause truncation if used with mismatched types, such as combining ints and floats improperly. When using compound assignment, ensure the expression on the right is the correct type. Use these operators to express incremental changes and to avoid repeating the variable name, which reduces copy-paste errors. Try converting a long-form assignment into a compound version and observe the result in the console. Assignment Operators and Shorthand means compound assignment like += and *= shorten code and reduce errors when updating variables incrementally.. In practical terms, keep code concise and expressive with compound assignments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Shorthand
keyIdea.text: Compound assignment like += and *= shorten code and reduce errors when updating variables incrementally.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Assignment Operators
Assignment Operators and Shorthand
Use compound operators to update variables clearly and concisely.
Examples
playerScore = playerScore + 10; // long form playerScore += 10; // shorthand playerHealth -= 20; // apply damage playerSpeed *= 1.2f; // speed boost
Tip
Prefer compound assignments when you update the same variable using a simple expression to reduce errors.
Warnings
  • Watch type compatibility when mixing ints and floats.
  • Remember that compound operators modify the original variable in place.
Key Takeaway

Use shorthand assignments to express intent and reduce duplicate variable names, but check type compatibility.

narration.text: Comparison operators compare values and return booleans that let your code branch. The common comparison operators are equals, not equals, less than, greater than, and their inclusive forms. For example, if (playerScore >= 100) checks whether the score reached the threshold. Logical operators combine these booleans. The AND operator requires both conditions to be true, while OR requires at least one, and NOT inverts a condition. A concrete example from the chapter is bool canMove = isAlive && (health > 0); which sets canMove true only when both isAlive and health positive are true. A frequent mistake is using = where == was intended inside conditionals, which assigns instead of comparing. Another subtle error is not grouping comparisons with parentheses when combining && and ||, which can lead to unexpected results. When writing conditions, state the intended truth test clearly and test with edge cases. Try writing an if statement that requires both a minimum score and a positive health to trigger a power-up. What combination of comparisons will capture that requirement reliably? Comparison and Logical Operators means use comparison operators to test values and logical operators to combine tests into clear conditions that drive game logic.. In practical terms, making decisions with ==, !=, <, >, &&, ||, and !. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision building
keyIdea.text: Use comparison operators to test values and logical operators to combine tests into clear conditions that drive game logic.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Comparison & Logical
Comparison and Logical Operators
Write clear conditions to control behavior at runtime.
Comparison Examples
  • playerScore >= 100
  • health == 0
  • playerName != ""
Logical Examples
  • isAlive && (health > 0)

screens.title: Scope: Local vs Member Variables
screens.subtitle: Where a variable can be accessed and why it matters

narration.text: Scope defines where a variable can be referenced in code. Member variables are declared on the class and can be used by any method within that class instance. Local variables are declared inside a method and exist only while that method runs. For example, public int playerScore declared on the class can be read or updated in Start(), Update(), and other methods. In contrast, int enemiesDefeated declared inside Start() cannot be accessed in Update(). Understanding scope prevents errors such as referencing an undefined variable or accidentally shadowing a class field with a local variable of the same name. Shadowing happens when a local variable uses the same name as a member variable and hides it inside the method, which can lead to confusing bugs. Best practice is to keep member variables for persistent state and use descriptive local names for temporary calculations. Additionally, avoid exposing internal implementation through public members; prefer methods to control access when needed. As a final check, ask whether a value needs to persist across frames. If it does, make it a member variable; if not, keep it local. Which variable in your code might be accidentally shadowed and how would you rename it to make intent clearer?

keyIdea.title: Scope matters
keyIdea.text: Use member variables for persistent state and local variables for temporary work. Avoid name shadowing to prevent subtle bugs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Scope
Scope: Local vs Member Variables
Decide where variables should live so you can access them where needed.
Member Variable
Declared on the class. Example: public int playerScore = 0; Accessible to all methods in the class and persists across frames.
Local Variable
Declared inside a method. Example: int enemiesDefeated = 0; Exists only while the method runs.
Best Practices
  • Make persistent state member variables.
  • Use local variables for temporary calculations.
  • Avoid reusing names that hide member variables to prevent shadowing bugs.

narration.text: Let's recap the three most important concepts from this chapter. First, a variable is a named storage place with a declared data type; choose the type to match the operations you need. Second, C# primitive types — int, float, bool, string — and Unity-specific structures like Vector3, Quaternion, and Color let you model game state and spatial information succinctly. Third, operators let you compute and test values: arithmetic for math, assignment to store results, comparison to produce booleans, and logical operators to combine tests. Also remember scope and access modifiers: member fields persist and can be exposed to the Inspector, while local variables are temporary. Watch for common pitfalls such as integer division truncation and confusing assignment with comparison inside a conditional. Use Inspector exposure to empower designers but keep implementation details private. With these core ideas you can declare, modify, and reason about variables in Unity C# confidently. What single change will you make to your variables after this review?

keyIdea.title: Three takeaways
keyIdea.text: Choose types that match use, prefer Unity structs for spatial data, and apply operators and scope rules carefully to avoid bugs.

narration.text: Keep a short mental checklist when you code. First, name variables clearly and pick a type that matches the value and operations. Second, use Vector3, Quaternion, and Color when dealing with positions, rotations, or color data so Unity methods accept values directly. Third, prefer public fields for values designers must tweak in the Inspector, and keep internal details private to prevent accidental misuse. Fourth, practice operators until you can spot when to use integer versus float arithmetic and when to combine comparison checks with logical operators. Finally, test edge cases like zero, negative values, and equality boundaries to avoid surprises.
